topics.title: Light rays and reflection by spherical mirrors

learn.hook: The dentist's small concave mirror and the convex mirror at a hilly hairpin bend in Uttarakhand obey the same two simple laws.
points: Light is electromagnetic radiation; the eye detects wavelengths from about 400 nm to 750 nm. Its speed in vacuum, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, is a fundamental constant.
Ray optics (geometrical optics): when the wavelength is tiny compared with the objects involved, light can be treated as travelling in straight lines called rays. A bundle of rays is a beam.
Laws of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
For a spherical mirror, the normal at any point is along the radius through that point (towards the centre of curvature).

Terms: pole P (centre of the mirror's surface), centre of curvature C, principal axis (line through P and C), aperture (size of the mirror). Paraxial rays are rays close to and nearly parallel to the principal axis.

example.q: A ray strikes a concave mirror at a point, making 25° with the radius drawn to that point. What is the angle of reflection?
steps: The radius is the normal at that point.
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence

learn.reallife: The convex mirrors fixed at sharp turns on mountain roads in Himachal Pradesh give drivers a wide view of oncoming traffic around the bend.

topics.title: Sign convention and the mirror equation

learn.hook: Mirror problems become simple arithmetic once you agree on one rule for signs. Physicists use the Cartesian sign convention, like a number line placed on the mirror's axis.
points: Cartesian sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive, below negative.
With light coming from the left, the object distance u is negative for real objects. Focal length of a concave mirror is negative; of a convex mirror, positive.
Focal length f = R/2 for spherical mirrors (paraxial rays).
Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, derived from similar triangles in a ray diagram.
Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image; positive m means a virtual, erect image.

example.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image position and magnification.
example.answer: v = -60 cm (real, in front); m = -2 (inverted, twice the size)

learn.reallife: Shaving and make-up mirrors are concave: placed within f of your face, they give an enlarged, erect, virtual image, matching m positive and greater than 1.

quiz.mistake: Thinks the relation is exact for all rays

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does my answer for a concave mirror come out negative?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Distances are measured from the pole; against the incident light is negative, so real images in front of a concave mirror get negative v. Sign sorted!
teach.nudge: Good! Which direction is positive in the Cartesian convention?

revise.summary: In the Cartesian sign convention distances are measured from the pole, positive along the incident light. Spherical mirrors have f = R/2 and obey 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, with magnification m = −v/u.
remember: Concave f < 0; convex f > 0; real object u < 0
m = −v/u: negative = real, inverted; positive = virtual, erect
traps: Don't solve first and add signs later; put the signs in before solving
f = R/2 does not hold for rays far from the axis; it holds only for paraxial rays

learn.hook: Where you place an object in front of a concave mirror decides whether you see a huge upright image, an upside-down one, or none at all.
points: Concave mirror, object beyond C: image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished.
Object at C: image at C, real, inverted, same size. Object between C and F: image beyond C, real, inverted, magnified.
Object at F: image at infinity. Object between F and P: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect, magnified.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F, whatever the object position.
Moving objects and rear-view mirrors: the image in a convex mirror moves much more slowly than the object; image speed ≈ (v/u)² × object speed.

example.q: A car 9 m behind a truck is seen in the truck's convex mirror of focal length 1 m. The car approaches at 10 m s⁻¹. How fast does its image move?

learn.reallife: The convex side-view mirrors on many cars and two-wheelers carry the warning 'objects in mirror are closer than they appear', because a convex mirror forms a diminished image.

teach.nudge: Good! What kind of mirror is it, and what kind of image does it make?

revise.summary: A concave mirror's image depends on object position: beyond C gives a small real image, at C same size, between C and F magnified real, at F at infinity, inside F magnified virtual. A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image.

learn.hook: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks bent at the surface. Light changes speed as it crosses from water to air, and that bends its path.
points: Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; and Snell's law: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ (a constant for the pair of media and a given colour).
Refractive index of medium 2 relative to 1: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂. Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
Going from rarer to denser (n₂₁ > 1), the ray bends towards the normal (r < i); from denser to rarer, it bends away from the normal.
Useful relations: n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁, and n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂.
Typical refractive indices: air 1.0003, water 1.33, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

example.q: Light travels from air into glass of refractive index 1.5. Find its speed in glass.

learn.reallife: Diamonds cut in Surat, India's diamond capital, sparkle partly because diamond's high refractive index (2.42) bends light strongly.

focus: Bending towards or away from the normal
remember: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂
traps: Frequency does not change on refraction
Going from denser to rarer, light does not bend towards the normal; it bends away

topics.title: Slabs, apparent depth and total internal reflection

learn.hook: A swimming pool always looks shallower than it is, and on a hot road you see 'water' that is not there. Both tricks come from refraction near a boundary.
points: Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral shift), which grows with slab thickness and angle of incidence.
Apparent depth (for near-normal viewing) = real depth/n. A pool 2 m deep in water (n = 4/3) looks 1.5 m deep. The normal shift is d(1 - 1/n).
Going from a denser to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle ic, the refraction angle is 90°.
Total internal reflection (TIR) happens when light goes from denser to rarer medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds ic. Then all light is reflected.
sin ic = 1/n₂₁ (n of denser relative to rarer). Critical angles: water 48.75°, crown glass about 41°, diamond about 24.4°.

example.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a 12 cm deep beaker of water (n = 4/3). How deep does it appear, and by how much is it raised?
example.answer: Appears 9 cm deep; raised by 3 cm

learn.reallife: Mirages on the Delhi-Jaipur highway in May are caused by refraction and total internal reflection of skylight in hot, less dense air near the road surface.

Answer: rays from outside are bent into a cone of half-angle equal to the critical angle

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'When does light get trapped inside water instead of coming out?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Going from denser to rarer at more than the critical angle, light is totally internally reflected. Trapped!
teach.nudge: Good! Two conditions are needed. What are they?

revise.summary: A glass slab shifts a ray sideways but keeps it parallel. Objects under water appear raised: apparent depth = real depth/n. Light going from denser to rarer beyond the critical angle (sin ic = 1/n) is totally internally reflected.
remember: TIR: denser → rarer and i > ic
traps: TIR cannot happen going from rarer to denser
A smaller critical angle does not mean less TIR; it means more (diamond sparkle)

topics.title: Total internal reflection at work: prisms and optical fibres

learn.hook: The broadband internet reaching Indian villages under BharatNet travels as light, bouncing through glass fibres thinner than a hair.
points: Activity: shine a laser pointer through slightly soapy or milky water in a glass and tilt it; beyond a certain angle the beam reflects completely at the surface. Safety: never look into or point a laser at anyone's eyes, and keep water away from electrical sockets.
Totally reflecting prisms (45°-90°-45° glass prisms, critical angle about 42°) turn rays through 90° (periscopes) or 180° (binoculars), and can invert images without changing size.
They reflect almost 100% of light, better than silvered mirrors.

Optical fibres: a glass or quartz core surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering the core undergoes repeated TIR and travels long distances with little loss, even when the fibre bends.
Uses: telecommunication (huge data rates), endoscopy (light pipes to see inside the body), and decorative lamps.

example.q: Why must the cladding of an optical fibre have a lower refractive index than the core?
steps: TIR needs light to go from denser to rarer medium.
The core must be denser than the cladding.
Then rays hitting the boundary beyond ic are totally reflected.
example.answer: So that light in the core is totally internally reflected at the core-cladding boundary

learn.reallife: Gastroenterologists in hospitals across India use endoscopes, bundles of optical fibres, to see inside a patient's stomach without surgery.

teach.praise: Chirp! Light hits the core-cladding boundary beyond the critical angle and is totally internally reflected again and again. Light pipe!
teach.nudge: Good! What keeps the light inside the core, and why must the core be denser?

revise.summary: Total internal reflection is used in 45°-90°-45° prisms to turn rays through 90° or 180°, reflecting almost all light, and in optical fibres, where light in a high-index core reflects repeatedly off lower-index cladding for communication and endoscopy.

topics.title: Refraction at spherical surfaces and the lens maker's formula

learn.hook: An air bubble in a glass paperweight looks bigger or smaller depending on where you look from. A single curved surface can act like a lens.
points: Refraction at a single spherical surface: n₂/v - n₁/u = (n₂ - n₁)/R, using the Cartesian sign convention (light from medium n₁ into n₂).
Applications: the apparent position of an object inside a glass sphere, or of an air bubble seen from outside.

A thin lens has two surfaces; combining the single-surface equation for both gives the lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n₂₁ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂), where n₂₁ is the lens material's index relative to the surroundings.
For a double convex lens, R₁ is positive and R₂ negative.
A lens in a different medium: its focal length changes because n₂₁ changes. A glass lens (n = 1.5) in water (n = 4/3) has f four times its value in air.

example.q: A double convex lens has R₁ = 20 cm and R₂ = -20 cm, with n = 1.5. Find f.

learn.reallife: Spectacle makers in Indian optical shops grind lens surfaces to specific radii; the lens maker's formula tells them which curvatures give the required power.

topics.title: Thin lens formula and power of a lens

learn.hook: An optometrist writes '-1.5 D' on your prescription. That number is the power of a lens, and it tells you exactly how strongly it bends light.
points: Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = v/u.
Convex (converging) lens: f > 0. Concave (diverging) lens: f < 0. Real images have v > 0 (on the other side); virtual images have v < 0.

Ray diagrams: a convex lens forms real, inverted images when the object is beyond F, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F. A concave lens always gives virtual, erect, diminished images.
Power P = 1/f (f in metres). Unit: dioptre (D), 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.
Converging lenses have positive power; diverging lenses have negative power.

example.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find v and m.

learn.reallife: Millions of Indians wear spectacles. A short-sighted student might need a -2 D concave lens, and a reader over 45 a +1.5 D convex lens.

topics.title: Combinations of lenses and optics problem practice

learn.hook: Camera and microscope objectives are not single lenses but stacks of them. Adding lenses is as easy as adding their powers.
points: Thin lenses in contact: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ...; equivalently P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
Total magnification of a combination: m = m₁m₂m₃...
Lenses at a separation: find the image by the first lens, then use it as the object for the second lens (measuring distances from the second lens).
Combining converging and diverging lenses of different glasses can reduce colour defects in cameras and microscopes.
Problem toolkit: mirror formula, lens formula, lens maker's formula, power, TIR condition, prism relations and instrument magnifications.

learn.hook: A prism bends light twice, once going in and once coming out. There is one special angle where the bending is the least, and it reveals the glass's refractive index.
points: For a triangular prism of angle A: r₁ + r₂ = A, where r₁ and r₂ are the refraction angles inside at the two faces.
Angle of deviation: δ = i + e - A, where i and e are the angles of incidence and emergence.
A graph of δ against i falls to a minimum Dm and then rises again.
At minimum deviation, i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2; the ray passes symmetrically. Then n₂₁ = sin[(A + Dm)/2]/sin(A/2).
For a thin prism (small A): δ = (n₂₁ - 1)A.

example.q: A prism of angle 60° gives minimum deviation 30°. Find n.

learn.reallife: Spectrometers in Indian research labs, like those at IIA Bengaluru, use prisms or gratings at minimum deviation to measure the refractive index and to split light into colours.

learn.hook: With a simple lens you can read the tiny print on a medicine strip. With two lenses, a pathologist at a district hospital can see the malaria parasite in a drop of blood.
points: Simple microscope (magnifier): a converging lens with the object within its focal length gives an erect, magnified, virtual image.
Angular magnification: m = 1 + D/f when the image is at the near point (D = 25 cm), and m = D/f when the image is at infinity (relaxed eye).
Compound microscope: an objective of short focal length forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image; the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier on it.
Magnifying power with the final image at infinity: m ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe), where L is the tube length (distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece).
To get high magnification, both fo and fe should be small.

example.q: A magnifier has f = 5 cm. Find the magnification with the image at the near point (25 cm) and at infinity.
example.answer: 6 at the near point; 5 at infinity

learn.reallife: Pathology labs across India use compound microscopes with 100× oil-immersion objectives and 10× eyepieces, giving a total magnification of about 1000×.

learn.hook: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune collects faint radio waves from space, while the optical telescopes at Devasthal in Uttarakhand gather faint light from galaxies billions of light years away.
points: Refracting astronomical telescope: an objective of large focal length and large aperture, and an eyepiece of short focal length. The objective forms a real image of a distant object at its focus.
Magnifying power in normal adjustment (final image at infinity): m = fo/fe. Tube length = fo + fe.
A larger objective aperture gathers more light (light-gathering power ∝ area ∝ D²) and gives better resolving power, so fainter and finer details are seen.

Reflecting telescopes (such as the Cassegrain design) use a concave primary mirror and a small convex secondary mirror. Advantages: no chromatic aberration, the mirror can be supported across its back, and large mirrors are cheaper and lighter than large lenses.
The image of a distant object (like the Moon) formed by the objective has size = fo × angle subtended by the object.

example.q: A telescope has fo = 100 cm and fe = 5 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length in normal adjustment.

learn.reallife: The 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital, India's largest, is a reflecting telescope. Its huge mirror gathers enough light to study faint stars and galaxies.
